summary:
NASA's MODIS sensors have tracked active fires for over two decades, but they are being retired, and their successor, VIIRS, sees fire differently: with smaller pixels, it detects almost four times more hotspots over the same area. Without a bridge, the fire history stops being comparable with today.

We built the Harmonized Burning Activity Calendar. A Python pipeline places 34 million NASA FIRMS hotspots for 14 South American countries (MODIS 2002–2020, VIIRS NOAA-20 2018–2025) on a common daily grid. Using the years when both sensors flew together, it works out what a VIIRS hotspot is worth in MODIS terms for each region and month. Tested on years it had never seen, the converted total was off by just 0.1%, and it tracked monthly country totals with R² = 0.99.

A web app turns the result into a 24-year calendar: pick a country or draw any area, compare any year with the 2002–2020 baseline, spot anomalies, and download the data. With it, emergency teams like CONAE's keep a consistent fire baseline after MODIS goes dark.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

The Harmonized Burning Activity Calendar turns two incompatible NASA fire records into one. MODIS (Terra and Aqua) observed active fires from 2002 to 2020. VIIRS (NOAA-20, 375 m) observes them from 2018 on, but detects almost four times more hotspots over the same area. Our system converts VIIRS into MODIS-equivalent hotspots and delivers a single, consistent series for South America from 2002 to 2025, explored through a web app.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Common grid: a Python pipeline reads 34 million hotspots from NASA FIRMS archives for 14 South American countries and counts them per 0.1° cell (about 11 km) per day, together with fire radiative power, day/night flag and confidence.

2. Conversion factor: in the overlap period (April 2018 to December 2020), we compute how many MODIS hotspots one VIIRS hotspot corresponds to, for each 2° region and each month of the year. Where data are sparse, the factor is pulled toward the continental value (0.26 MODIS hotspots per VIIRS hotspot), so quiet places do not get noisy factors.

3. Testing: we compared nine variants of this conversion, plus nonlinear models, by fitting on two overlap years and testing on the third, repeated for each year. The selected model tracked monthly country totals with R² = 0.99 and cell-by-month values with R² = 0.80, and the converted total was off by only 0.1%.

4. Harmonized series: MODIS is kept as observed through 2020, and VIIRS is converted from 2021 on. Every converted value carries an uncertainty taken from those tests.

5. Web app: a FastAPI service answers most queries in under 0.1 s, and a React app shows a years-by-months calendar (activity, or anomaly versus the 2002-2020 average), a map of where it burned, a day-by-day calendar, the seasonal cycle, annual totals with uncertainty bars, and CSV downloads. Users pick a country or draw any area on the map.

BENEFITS

- One baseline from 2002 to today, so a season can be called normal or abnormal regardless of which satellite saw it. Example: 2024 appears as the 3rd most active fire year in South America since 2002, 36% above the 2002-2020 average.

- Fires do not follow borders: any area can be analyzed, not only countries.

- Trust through transparency: for 2018-2020 the app shows converted VIIRS next to observed MODIS, so users can check the validation themselves.

- Raw MODIS and VIIRS counts are kept in every export.

INTENDED IMPACT

Keep burning activity calendars alive for emergency teams such as CONAE's after MODIS is switched off, and give fire managers and researchers a consistent record to follow trends and anomalies as fire weather becomes more frequent and intense. The pipeline is generic: changing the country list runs it for any region of the world.

CREATIVE ASPECTS

- We treat the two satellites like two currencies. The "exchange rate" between them changes with place and season, so we estimate it per region and month instead of using one global number.

- We convert VIIRS into MODIS units, not the reverse: the 19-year history is MODIS, and detections MODIS never made cannot be invented.

- We let the data decide. The intuitive idea of merging 375 m VIIRS pixels into 1 km clusters to imitate MODIS did not improve results, and nonlinear models performed worse. We report both findings.

- Validation and uncertainty are part of the product, not hidden in a report.
